Module 3 - Teacher Standards Map (INTERNAL ONLY)

English IV (1001400) Standard base, shared with Honors (1001410 overlay) | Q3 Module 3: What We Become | Florida B.E.S.T. ELA (CPALMS 1001400) + Texas TEKS 19 TAC §110.39

Do not put this file, or any code in it, on a student-facing page. Standards are tracked here only. Model: the 10th-grade M2_teacher_Standards_Map.md.

Mapped against the built pages (verified 2026-10-13), not the build spec. Every row names a file that exists in Semester 2_Final\Module 3 - What We Become\ or project-lessons\, by the title on the page; graded items also carry their Canvas assignment name. Each benchmark claim was checked against that item's content.

Sources read for this map. Florida: the CPALMS course export English 4 (1001400).docx (generated 5/18/2026), benchmark text and clarifications. Texas: 19 TAC §110.39, English IV (adopted 2017, amended eff. 8/1/2019), read in full from the Cornell LII copy of the rule on 2026-10-13. The local TEKS English 4 standards.pdf is a scanned image with no text layer (no text from pdftotext or PyMuPDF), so student-expectation letters below are cited from the LII text; the Semester 1 audit Semester 1_Final\_STANDARDS-AUDIT_English4_FL-TEKS.md was read for the strand ratings and gap history. Mississippi (diocesan = CCSS): no Semester 1 map with a CCSS crosswalk exists in this course folder, so CCSS is omitted here.

1. Course benchmark reference (CPALMS 1001400, "2024 - And Beyond")

Every benchmark below is rated Major for this course except the six ELA.K12.EE benchmarks (Supporting). Short forms; read the CPALMS text for clarifications.

5. Gaps and honest limits for Module 3

  • TEKS 7(C), drama: not covered. Module 3 has no dramatic text, and neither does Module 4 or Semester 1. The Semester 1 audit proposed Everyman or a single Shakespeare scene study; neither is in this build. The gap stays open at the course level.
  • R.3.3 (classic influence on contemporary world texts): not claimed in M3. Kafka (1915) and the public-domain authors here are not contemporary world texts in the CPALMS sense (written after WWII). The Frankenstein look-backs are cross-text work, not R.3.3. The course's R.3.3 carrier is Module 4.
  • C.4.1 (research) and the C.1.3 clarification ("thorough research"): nothing in M3 requires outside sources; the Module 3 Project is text-based. TEKS 11 likewise has no new coverage here. The Q1 Studio brief carries C.4.1 for the year. Adding a one-or-two verified-source requirement to the project's argument formats would close this; flagged for the lead.
  • TEKS 10(F), composed rhetorical analysis: not built. Studio Session 3 and E3 apply kairos and the fallacy check to the student's own pitch, which is applied work, not a composed analysis of a published speech.
  • R.3.4 is partial. Antithesis (Emerson) and irony (Kafka) are taught as devices within one text each; no item evaluates rhetorical choices across several published texts. The Week 8 synthesis lessons compare arguments (R.2.4) more than rhetoric.
  • R.2.1 (evaluate structures/features, say how the text could be more effective): not claimed. The lessons discuss form (the Meditations as private notes, the ragged form of "The Collar") but never ask for an evaluation of informational structures or features.
  • EE.4.1 / TEKS 1(D), collaboration: no discussion forum or group deliverable; both wrappers state this. Structural limit of the solo asynchronous model.
  • R.1.4 note: context cards give period, publication and scope of work; none includes critical reception at the time.
  • TEKS 7(A) note: British literature here is Herbert (1633) and Blake (1794); Mansfield (New Zealand-born) and Joyce (Irish) are not counted as British.
  • Florida version requirement ("approximately one-third of the titles from the 12th Grade Sample Book List"): the list is not in the project folder, so compliance is not verified here.
  • Kafka text rule: no quotation of any English translation appears on any M3 page; R.3.2 evidence is paraphrase by design.

1. Module 4 coverage at a glance (as built)

Module 4 is the course's post-WWII anchor and its call-to-duty module: The Fellowship of the Ring (Tolkien, 1954; in copyright; read in the student's own copy; short analytical quotations only, never embedded) from the Prologue through Book II, Chapter 10, with Plato's Cave (Wk 1) and Hughes's "Epilogue" ("I, Too") (Wk 4) as public-domain lens texts, then a year-synthesis lesson in Week 9. The frame as built: the Company is neither chosen nor inherited; each member comes by an individual call that joins personal purpose, loyalty to a people, and a higher call to what is right; the Ring is everyone's problem and no one people's to carry, and Elrond will not lay it on anyone.

4. Gaps and honest limits for Module 4

  • R.3.3, classic influence on contemporary world texts: partial. The Fellowship (1954) is a contemporary world text in the CPALMS sense, and Plato's Cave (Classical period) is read against it in "The Shire and the Cave" and QW "Comfort or Cave?". The lessons use Plato as a lens and test where the comparison breaks; they do not trace a documented influence of Plato, or of the Old English and Norse literature Tolkien studied, on the book. "An Ordinary Hobbit" states Tolkien's scholarship as a fact only. Count this as partial credit, not a full match.
  • TEKS 7(C), drama: not covered. There is no dramatic text in Module 4, Module 3, or Semester 1. The Semester 1 audit proposed Everyman or a single Shakespeare scene; neither is in this build. The gap stays open at the course level.
  • C.4.1 (research), the C.1.3 clarification, and TEKS 11: no new research requirement. The Module 4 Project is text-based (the Fellowship plus at least one other text from the year). The Final Pitch requires every number to be sourced and grades sourcing under "Polish and precision", but reuses the Q1 Studio research; no new sources are required.
  • TEKS 10(F), composed rhetorical analysis: not built. Studio Session 4 and the Final Pitch apply persuasion to the student's own pitch.
  • R.3.4 is partial. Antithesis is taught on Tolkien sentences here and on Emerson in M3, but no single item evaluates rhetorical choices across published texts, and Studio Session 4 does not teach the appeals by name.
  • R.2.x (nonfiction argument): not claimed in M4 beyond the light R.2.4 review in "What We Owe". R.2.2 to R.2.4 are carried in Module 3 (Emerson, Marcus) and Semester 1.
  • R.1.4: one poet in context this module (Hughes); the context card has no critical-reception material. Herbert reappears only on the Recitation Q4 menu.
  • EE.4.1 / TEKS 1(D), collaboration: no discussion forum or group deliverable in the module or either wrapper. Structural limit of the solo asynchronous model.
  • Florida version requirement ("approximately one-third of the titles from the 12th Grade Sample Book List"): not verified, because the list is not in the project folder.
  • Copyright: Tolkien appears only as short marked analytical quotations (at most 35 words each, at most 150 per page), never embedded; students read in their own copy. Recitation Q4 uses no Tolkien.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write one argument of 250 to 350 words about who or what is responsible for what Gregor becomes in Part I. Weigh three candidates: the change itself, the firm he works for, and his family. Name your position in the first sentence.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Who made Gregor what he is: the change, the firm, or the family?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
State your position in the first sentence: the one you hold most responsible, or how you divide the blame among the three.
2
Use Part I. Describe two moments by what happens and where, such as his worry about the missed train, the chief clerk's visit, or the father driving him back into his room. Quote a few words from your copy only if they carry the point, and cite the part.
3
State the strongest case for a different answer fairly, then answer it.
4
Write one sentence that gives Gregor's thought in the narrator's voice without a tag such as “he thought” (free indirect discourse).
5
Use at least two of this week’s Word Study words, used accurately.

The first sentence names who or what is most responsible, or how blame divides.
☐
Two moments from Part I are described accurately and tied to the claim.
☐
The strongest other answer is stated fairly, then answered.
☐
One sentence uses free indirect discourse.
☐
At least two Word Study words are used accurately, and the writing is 250 to 350 words.

Four options, equal weight
 
Record one. About 3 minutes.
1Oral Book ResponseABOUT 3 MINUTES
Answer these five out loud, in order. Notes are fine; a script read word for word is not.
›What is the book, and how far did the reading get?
›Pick one character. What does the character want, and what is in the way?
›Describe a moment where that character makes a choice the reader would not have made. Why did the character make it?
›Read one marked sentence or short passage, and say why that one.
›Who should read this book, and who should skip it?
2Dramatic ReadingABOUT 3 MINUTES
›Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
›Read it aloud as that character. Decide before recording what the character wants in this moment, then let pace, volume and pauses show it.
›Then talk for about a minute: who the character is, what the character wants here, and what the voice did to show it. Name one specific choice.

›Answer the strongest objection. State it fairly first, then answer it.
›Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4A Different EndingABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only for a book that was finished. An ending cannot be replaced if it was never reached.
›Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate.
›Name the exact point where the new version branches off, then describe the new ending in detail: what happens, to whom, and how it finishes.
›Explain why the new ending is truer to what the book has been about. Name the idea or theme it serves.
›Say what the new ending costs. Name what is lost by not keeping the author's ending.

quizzes.title: Module 3 Opening Questions: What We Become
quizzes.description:
Welcome to Module 3: What We Become.

For the next nine weeks the reading follows a self that is alone. Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis shuts a man in his room, two short stories put a woman and a boy by themselves in a crowd, and two thinkers and three poets ask how far a person can stand on his or her own. The module ends with a project of your own choosing on what makes a monster and what makes us human.

What makes a monster, and what makes us human?

Answer the few questions below before starting. This is a starting point, and the first question returns at the end of the module to show how thinking has changed.

Welcome to Module 4: The Fellowship of the Ring.

For the next nine weeks the reading follows a company that forms around one object. J. R. R. Tolkien's The Fellowship of the Ring begins in a comfortable corner of the world, moves through places that offer welcome and danger, and arrives at a Council where a problem that belongs to everyone has to be carried by someone. The module ends with a project of your own choosing on what we owe when a problem belongs to everyone.

What do we owe when a problem belongs to everyone?

Answer the few questions below before starting. This is a starting point, and the first question returns at the end of the module and the year.
